write.desc: The set structure of the real line (open and closed sets, limit points, closure, compactness, connectedness, perfect sets) belongs together because these ideas give the exact hypotheses later used by the big theorems on continuous functions, and compactness in particular is how local information becomes global.

points.name: Neighbourhoods and open sets
points.what: The learner can define the epsilon-neighbourhood V_epsilon(a) = (a - epsilon, a + epsilon) and an open set (every point has a neighbourhood inside the set), and prove that open intervals, R and the empty set are open while [0,1) is not.
outside: absolute value as distance and the triangle inequality

points.name: Limit points and isolated points
points.what: The learner can define a limit (accumulation) point of a set (every neighbourhood meets the set at a point other than x) and an isolated point, find them for sets like {1/n}, Z and Q, and prove that x is a limit point of A exactly when x is the limit of a sequence of points of A different from x.
outside: epsilon-N definition of the limit of a sequence

points.name: Closed sets
points.what: The learner can define a closed set as one containing all its limit points, prove that a set is closed exactly when its complement is open and exactly when every convergent sequence in it has its limit in it, and classify examples such as [a,b], Z, {1/n} (not closed) and Q (neither open nor closed).

points.name: Closure and interior
points.what: The learner can form the closure of a set (the set together with its limit points) and its interior, prove that the closure is the smallest closed set containing the set and the interior the largest open set inside it, and compute examples such as the closure of Q being R.

points.name: Unions and intersections of open and closed sets
points.what: The learner can prove that any union and any finite intersection of open sets is open, deduce the matching facts for closed sets by De Morgan's laws, and give counterexamples such as the intersection of (-1/n, 1/n) being {0} to show the finiteness condition is needed.
outside: indexed unions and intersections of sets
De Morgan's laws for indexed families of sets

points.name: Compact sets by sequences
points.what: The learner can state the sequential definition of compactness (every sequence in K has a subsequence converging to a point of K) and prove, using Bolzano-Weierstrass, that a subset of R is compact in this sense exactly when it is closed and bounded.

points.name: Open covers and finite subcovers
points.what: The learner can define an open cover of a set and a finite subcover, state the open-cover definition of compactness, and check directly whether a given cover has a finite subcover.
outside: indexed families of sets and their unions

points.name: Why (0,1) and R are not compact
points.what: The learner can show with both definitions why (0,1) and R fail to be compact: the sequence 1/n has no subsequence converging in (0,1) and the cover by (1/n, 1) has no finite subcover, while R has the sequence n and the cover by (-n, n); and can say which of closedness or boundedness fails in each case.

points.name: The Heine-Borel theorem
points.what: The learner can state and prove that for a subset K of R the three conditions are equivalent: K is sequentially compact, K is closed and bounded, and every open cover of K has a finite subcover, including the bisection (nested interval) argument that a closed bounded set has the finite subcover property.

points.name: Nested compact sets
points.what: The learner can prove that a decreasing sequence of nonempty compact sets has a nonempty intersection, and show by examples such as (0, 1/n) and [n, infinity) that both closedness and boundedness are needed.

points.name: Compactness turns local into global
points.what: The learner can explain and use the main idea behind compactness: if every point of a compact set has a neighbourhood where some property holds (such as meeting a set in only finitely many points, or a bound), finitely many such neighbourhoods cover the set, so the property holds on the whole set; and can see why this argument breaks down on (0,1).

points.name: Separated sets and connectedness
points.what: The learner can define separated sets (neither meets the closure of the other) and connected and disconnected sets, and prove that sets such as Q and (0,1) union (1,2) are disconnected.

points.name: Connected subsets of R are the intervals
points.what: The learner can prove that a subset of R is connected exactly when it is an interval, that is, whenever a < c < b with a and b in the set, c is in the set, using the supremum to find the point where a separation would have to break.

points.name: The Cantor set
points.what: The learner can construct the Cantor set by removing middle thirds, prove that it is closed and compact, that the removed intervals have total length 1, and that it contains no interval, and find points in it other than the endpoints (such as 1/4).

points.name: Perfect sets
points.what: The learner can define a perfect set (closed with no isolated points), prove that the Cantor set is perfect, and prove with nested compact sets that every nonempty perfect set is uncountable, so the Cantor set is uncountable despite having length zero.

points.name: Beyond the real line: metric spaces
points.what: The learner knows that neighbourhoods, open and closed sets, compactness and connectedness use only a distance function and so make sense in any metric space, and that Heine-Borel can fail there (for example, a closed bounded infinite set with the discrete metric is not compact).
